newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Baltic central bankers say banking sectors healthy.
newsitem.headline: Baltic central bankers say banking sectors healthy.

text.p: Baltic central bankers said on Thursday that the banking sectors in their countries were becoming increasingly competitive and transparent, reducing the risk that the crises which have shaken them in the past will be repeated.

"The crisis in 1995 (in Latvia) was the final clearing out of the banking system," Latvian central bank governor Einars Repshe told a Euromoney conference on capital markets and investment in the Baltics.
"It cleaned out the bad, uncompetitive banks and left the good ones," he said.
Latvia, like Baltic neighbours Estonia and Lithuania, experienced a painful shock to its banking system which shook public confidence in the sector and stalled economic recovery.
Estonia had the first case of the banking blues in 1992, when several of its banks went bust.
Latvia's banking sector was hit in 1995, when Banka Baltija, the largest bank in the Baltics at the time, collapsed.
Lithuania followed in late 1995, when two of its top banks were unexpectedly shut.
In all three countries, poor credit policies, insider lending, and dubious book-keeping brought down several banks.
But central bankers said that they had learned from the hard lessons of the past.
"The central banks and commercial banks in Lithuania have learned their lessons from the crisis," Lithuanian central bank governor Reinoldijus Sharkinas told the conference.
"We have successfully insisted on the introduction of international accounting standards and all banks are following them," Sharkinas said.
"Greater transparency will help increase public confidence," he said.
"In Latvia, we have a very well provisioned and open system...What you see on the balance sheet reflects reality," he said.
He added that the central bank would take a tough line with insolvent banks.
"There will be no bail-outs for Latvian banks."
His comments were echoed by Peter Lohmus, the deputy governor of the Bank of Estonia.
"In 1992, we gave a clear signal that we would not save bad banks...our commercial banks got the message, and have become very competitive as a result," he said.
The central bankers also said that they expected further consolidation.
The number of banks in Estonia has fallen from over 40 in 1992 to 14. In Lithuania, the number of banks has fallen over the past two years from 27 to 12.
Latvia has 32 banks, down from close to 50 three years ago.
"I do foresee some mergers as minimum capital requirements are raised... smaller banks will have to capitalise or join capital," said Latvia's Repshe.
